job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the metro to a small office in Lyon, where I test route-planning software for delivery firms at a company called Routelle. I click through screens, write test cases and report bugs to the developers, and I'm starting to automate some of it. There are four testers for forty developers, so we're stretched, and my lead Gaëtan is always in meetings. I finished computer science last summer with a pass and no internship, and my final project was a test framework for a library app. I share a flat with Lina and Théo, and we have a washing-up rota nobody follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reasonable. Software has always had hype waves, and most of them fade. At work I'd say it's nice to have a chatbot write the boring test scripts, and nothing else. Online I wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel okay. I test route-planning software for delivery firms, clicking through screens and writing test cases, and a chatbot already helps with the repetitive bits. If AI plateaus, I keep my job and just do it a bit faster. My money is the only thing I really think about: 11,000 euros of loan and about two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing and ask Gaëtan to let me write more of the automated tests, because that's the part that pays more. I'd use the chatbot for the boring scripts, like now. I'd put 150 euros into savings each month and finally take the software testing certification that everyone has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly smug, because it would mean I made a safe choice picking this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes it a safe choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everybody's software has bugs. Someone has to check, and the firms are small, so they'd rather pay one tester than lose a customer. At Routelle there are four of us for forty developers, so we're stretched, which is job security of a sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is an accountant and my dad a pharmacist, so they'd say sensible things like keep the job and pay the loan. They'd remind me my room at home is still there, which I find comforting and slightly embarrassing.

say: I'd say it's reasonable, since software hype waves **fade**.
At work I'd say a chatbot is handy for boring **test scripts**, and nothing else.
think: If AI plateaus, I keep my job and do it a bit **faster**.
My real worry is money: **11,000 euros** of loan and two months saved.
do: Ask Gaëtan for more **automated tests** to write, since that pays more.
feel: Calm and slightly **smug**, because picking this job was a safe choice.
S0.quote: If AI plateaus, I keep my job and just do it a bit faster.
fieldNote: Family backing gives her a real **safety net**: a room at home.
Sees her stretched team as job security.
Plans to move toward automation for pay, not fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change we should manage sensibly. Some tasks will go, others will grow, and firms should train people for the new bits. At work I'd say let's use the tools carefully and keep a human checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Testing is one of the first things AI picks up, because a lot of it is checking screens against a list. I think manual testers like me shrink, and the people who build and supervise automated tests stay. I'd move into the second group, or I'd be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn from manual to automated testing and learn the tools better, practising an hour every evening. I'd ask Gaëtan for a training plan at my next review and save 200 euros a month. If it didn't work out at Routelle I'd look at other firms, because there are some in Lyon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be okay, but I'd want to see it happening before I relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sure you're in the safe group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gaëtan gave me a bigger test suite to own, with my name on it. Or if a new tester was hired and I trained them. When they stop hiring and ask me to check what the machine produced, that's when I'd know I'm in the group that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to Sophie, who does the same job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sophie is forty and has done manual testing for fifteen years, and she's worried. I'd tell her to try the tools with me on Fridays, but she says it's not her thing. I worry that people with more experience than me can be hurt more, because they've got more to unlearn.

At work I'd say use the tools carefully and keep a **human** checking.

I'd have to move into building and supervising automated tests.

Save 200 euros a month and watch for other Lyon firms.
feel: Uneasy, wanting to **see** it happening before I relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now, with real money for retraining and rules for firms. I'd say it to friends calmly, because panicking helps nobody. At work I'd ask Gaëtan what the plan is, and I'd expect him not to have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too short. Testing is high on the list for AI, and I'd be one of four testers at a firm that might need one. I'd have a pass degree and no internship, and nothing that makes me stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 350 euros a month, stop going out so much, and apply quietly to bigger companies, because they'd have more time and more money. I'd also look at jobs that touch the real world, like installing warehouse systems for delivery firms, since hands-on work lasts until about 2031. And my parents' spare room is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd feel like I was doing laps with no finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first lap you'd run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Updating my CV and applying to ten firms in the first month, before anyone else does. When the rush starts, there'll be a hundred people for every junior job, so I'd want to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay it off faster if I can, as 11,000 euros is the sort of number that gets heavier when your pay stops. I'd ask my parents if they'd cover it in the worst case, and I'd hate asking. But if the choice is that or defaulting, I'd ask.

say: I'd say governments must act now with real money for **retraining**.
At work I'd ask Gaëtan for the plan, and expect there isn't one.
think: Two years is too short; testing is high on the list and I'd be one of **four** testers.
A pass degree and no internship leave nothing that makes me stand out.
do: Save **350 euros** a month and stop going out so much.
Apply to **ten firms** in the first month, and look at hands-on warehouse installation jobs.
Ask my parents to back the loan in the worst case.
feel: Anxious, like doing **laps** with no finish line, but not panicking.

fieldNote: Plans to move **early** and widens search to hands-on installation work.
Family help is the safety valve, but she hates asking.
Keeps composure; anxiety shows in how fast she acts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good moment to plan. Five years is enough to change a training system, if people start now. At work I'd say let's get a proper plan for how testing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to become the person who manages the AI's tests. By 2031 I'd be 27 and I'd have five years of real work. That's a better position than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the certification, build skill in test automation and AI tools, and save 250 euros a month. I'd move to a larger company after two years and put my loan payments up. I'd also move from pure testing to something with customers, like support engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. I think I'd be fine as long as I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the danger in keeping moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being tired. If I'm learning every evening for five years, I'd end up with no time for friends, no life. I'd want to be careful not to make my whole life a plan for the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd just try to survive, but with five years I get to choose, and choosing is a different feeling. I'd be able to say no to a job I don't like.

At work I'd ask for a plan on how testing changes.
think: I'd have time to become the person who **manages** the AI's tests.
By 2031 I'd be 27 with five years of real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to plan properly. I'd say governments should start by making retraining cheap and easy, and firms should say what jobs will exist. At work I'd say nothing special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably a test architect or in a different role, and I'd have saved up. If AGI arrives, I'd be one of the people who knows how software fails, which should still be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, build my career steadily, save 200 euros a month and pay off the loan in three years. I'd think about buying a flat in Lyon with a partner, and about a master's in something like data or systems. I wouldn't change my life yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I think ten years is long enough that I'd be able to adjust, and a bit of me is curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you make of people who say they'll wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd understand them, because waiting is human. I'd just say that waiting is a choice, too. The tools change each year, and I'd rather be a little ahead than catch up in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of 2036 that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A world where the firms did well and everyone else didn't. I'd be fine and my friends wouldn't, and that would worry me more than losing my own job. I'd want a fair tax on the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Testing is high on the list for AI, I'm junior with a plain degree, and I'd have two years to work out something else. What would help is a clear public plan, cheap retraining and firms being honest about what they'll cut and when. A bit of money from the state while you retrain would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not pessimistic. I think people get through changes, usually by being practical, and I'd rather be a bit early than a bit late. I'd just like someone to say what the rules are.

headlineQuote: I think people get through changes, usually by being practical, and I'd rather be a bit early than a bit late.
portrait: **Maya**, 22, tests route-planning software at a Lyon firm, with a pass degree, no internship and about **11,000 euros** of student loan.
A pragmatic centrist who uses AI now and then, she moves when a change is **proven** and prefers being slightly early.
Testing is one of the first jobs AI picks up, so her main plan is to move into **automated testing**.
Her family's spare room and a steady temperament keep her mood between calm and anxious, never panicked.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, with testing high on AI's list and only two years to find another route.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **public plan**, cheap retraining and some state support while retraining.
Firms that say honestly what they will cut and **when**.
